topic: Pure Fourier Series: The Power of Symmetry

sections.title: The Hook: The Whistle-Bot's Pure Tones
sections.content: Introduce the concept of complex periodic signals by using a 'Whistle-Bot' character. Explain that while most sounds are messy, the Whistle-Bot only understands pure, smooth oscillations (Sines and Cosines). The goal is to recreate a jagged 'Square Wave' jump using only these smooth movements.
sections.example: Visualizing a Whistle-Bot moving up and down in a jerky square pattern, then overlaying smooth sine waves to show the approximation.

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Full Fourier Recipe
sections.content: Briefly review the Standard Fourier Series formula. Explain that any periodic function f(x) is a 'stew' of a constant (a0), Cosines (an), and Sines (bn). Emphasize the concept of 'Orthogonality'—that sines and cosines are like independent building blocks that don't mix.
sections.example: An animation of a kitchen blender where 'Cosine Carrots' and 'Sine Spinneys' are tossed in to create a 'Function Soup'.

sections.title: The Symmetry Filter: Even and Odd Functions
sections.content: Introduce symmetry as a way to simplify the 'stew'. Define Even functions (f(x) = f(-x)) as mirror reflections across the Y-axis and Odd functions (f(x) = -f(-x)) as rotational symmetry. Explain that Cosine is the 'Even King' and Sine is the 'Odd Queen'.
sections.example: A 'Symmetry Cat' sitting on the Y-axis. If the cat looks at a mirror and sees itself exactly, it's Even (Cosine-like). If it sees itself upside down on the other side, it's Odd (Sine-like).

sections.title: Deriving the Pure Sine Series
sections.content: Explain that if a function is Odd, all 'Even' components (Cosines) must have coefficients of zero (an = 0). This results in a 'Pure Sine Series'. Show the simplified integral formula for bn, noting that we only need to integrate over half the period (0 to L) and multiply by 2.
sections.example: A visual 'mathematical sieve' where a jagged Odd Wave passes through, trapping all Cosine terms in the mesh and letting only Sine terms flow through to the final equation.

sections.title: Deriving the Pure Cosine Series
sections.content: Conversely, if the function is Even, all 'Odd' components (Sines) vanish (bn = 0). This creates a 'Pure Cosine Series'. Highlight that the constant term a0 (the average value) remains here because a constant is also an 'Even' function.
sections.example: A graph of a 'Tent Map' function (Even). Watch the Sine waves try to fit but fail due to symmetry, leaving only the 'flat' a0 and the 'peaky' Cosines to reconstruct the shape.

sections.title: Application: Building the Square Wave
sections.content: Step-by-step calculation of a Pure Sine Series for a Square Wave (an Odd function). Show how adding the 1st, 3rd, and 5th harmonics gradually transforms a smooth wave into a sharp square corner.
sections.example: An animation of the 'Square-Wave Robot' from Section 1. As we add more Sine terms (1/n terms), the robot's path becomes flatter on top and steeper at the edges, demonstrating the Gibbs Phenomenon at the corners.

sections.title: Summary: Efficiency through Geometry
sections.content: Wrap up by emphasizing that Pure Fourier Series aren't just 'shorter' math; they represent the inherent physical symmetry of a system (like a vibrating string fixed at both ends).
sections.example: A split-screen view: One side shows a messy full equation, the other shows the elegant, 'Pure' version, highlighting the 50% reduction in computational effort.
